topic.subject: general
topic.title: Saving and budgeting
topic.scope: needs vs wants, making a budget, saving first, piggy bank vs bank account, small savings growing over time

nodes.name: Making a budget
external_prereqs: addition and subtraction of whole numbers

nodes.name: Saving habits and places to save
Wants are things we would like but can live without
Same item can be a need or a want depending on situation
Money is limited so choices must be made
Income is the money coming in
Expenses are the money going out
Set aside savings as soon as money arrives
Saving is regular, even if small
A piggy bank holds cash at home, with no interest and risk of loss
A bank account keeps money safe and you can withdraw it
Small regular amounts add up over time

misconceptions.statement: Anything I use every day is a need.
misconceptions.why: Daily habits feel essential, so frequency is confused with necessity.
misconceptions.fix: A need is something required to live and be healthy, like food, water, clothing and shelter. Using something daily, like a video game, does not make it a need.

probe.question: Rahul plays a mobile game every day. Is the game a need or a want?
probe.wrong_answer: A need, because he uses it every day.

misconceptions.root_belief: frequent use means it is essential

misconceptions.statement: Needs are only food.
misconceptions.why: Food is the most obvious daily need, so other needs like clothing, shelter, health and education are overlooked.
misconceptions.fix: Needs include food, clothing, shelter, healthcare and basic education, not only food.

probe.question: Which of these is a need: a school uniform, a toy, or chocolate?
probe.wrong_answer: Chocolate, because it is food and only food is a need.

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar example represents the whole category

misconceptions.statement: Wants are bad and should never be bought.
misconceptions.why: Adults telling children not to waste money makes wants seem wrong.
misconceptions.fix: Wants are fine in moderation once needs are met and savings are set aside. A budget can include a small amount for wants.

probe.question: After paying for needs and saving, Meena has Rs 50 left. Should she spend it on an ice cream?
probe.wrong_answer: No, wants should never be bought.

misconceptions.root_belief: if something is limited it is forbidden

misconceptions.statement: If something is a need for one person it is a need for everyone in every situation.
misconceptions.why: Students expect fixed lists of needs and wants.
misconceptions.fix: Whether something is a need depends on the situation. A bicycle is a want for a child who lives near school but a need for one who must cycle 6 km to school.

probe.question: A bicycle is a need for Asha who lives 6 km from school. Is it a need for Ravi who lives next door to school?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a bicycle is a need for everyone.

misconceptions.root_belief: a category is the same in every context

misconceptions.statement: If it is expensive it must be a need, and if it is cheap it must be a want.
misconceptions.why: Price is mistaken for importance.
misconceptions.fix: Need or want depends on whether it is required for living, not on its price. Salt is cheap but a need; a costly watch is a want.

probe.question: Is a Rs 5000 branded shoe a need and a Rs 20 notebook for school a want?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the costly shoe is a need and the cheap notebook is a want.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more importance

misconceptions.statement: If I earn enough, I can buy everything I want, so choices are not needed.
misconceptions.why: Children see adults buying many things and assume money is unlimited.
misconceptions.fix: Everyone's money is limited compared with everything they might want, so everyone must choose what to buy first.

probe.question: Why does a family with a good salary still need to make a budget?
probe.wrong_answer: They don't need to, they have enough for everything.

misconceptions.root_belief: rich people have no limits
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's understanding of scarcity and economic concepts

misconceptions.statement: Wants should be bought first because they make us happy.
misconceptions.why: Immediate pleasure feels more urgent than long-term needs.
misconceptions.fix: Needs come first because they keep us healthy and safe. Wants can be bought only with money left after needs and savings.

probe.question: Meera has Rs 100. She needs a notebook for Rs 40. A toy costs Rs 80. What should she buy first?
probe.wrong_answer: The toy, because it makes her happy.

misconceptions.root_belief: what feels urgent is what matters most

misconceptions.statement: Income means only a salary.
misconceptions.why: Salary is the common example of earning.
misconceptions.fix: Income is any money received, such as salary, pocket money, gifts, business profit, rent or farm sales.

probe.question: Kabir gets Rs 200 pocket money and Rs 100 from his uncle. What is his income this month?
probe.wrong_answer: Zero, because he has no salary.

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar example represents the whole category

misconceptions.statement: Only big purchases count as expenses.
misconceptions.why: Small payments feel too minor to notice.
misconceptions.fix: Every amount spent is an expense, including small ones like snacks or bus fare, and small expenses add up.

probe.question: Rohan spends Rs 20 daily on snacks. How much is this expense in 30 days?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, it is too small to count as an expense.

misconceptions.root_belief: small amounts have no effect

misconceptions.statement: A budget is a list of what I already spent.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse a plan with a record.
misconceptions.fix: A budget is a plan made before spending, showing how much to spend and save. A record of past spending is an account of expenses.

probe.question: When is a budget made: before or after spending the money?
probe.wrong_answer: After, to note down what was spent.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Savings are what is left over after I spend as I like.
misconceptions.why: Most people observe saving as leftover money.
misconceptions.fix: Savings is income minus expenses, but good savers decide the savings amount first and spend the rest, otherwise little is left.

probe.question: Anu gets Rs 500 and spends freely. Should she plan her savings before or after spending?
probe.wrong_answer: After, she should save whatever is left.

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual way is the best way
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's and adults' saving behaviour in financial literacy research

misconceptions.statement: Spending more than my income is fine because I can always borrow.
misconceptions.why: Borrowing seems to make the shortfall vanish.
misconceptions.fix: Spending more than income creates debt that must be repaid, often with interest, so a good budget keeps expenses within income.

probe.question: Income is Rs 5000 and planned expenses are Rs 6000. Is this budget good?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the extra Rs 1000 can be borrowed so there is no problem.

misconceptions.root_belief: a problem that is postponed is solved

misconceptions.statement: Once a budget is made it should never be changed.
misconceptions.why: A plan is treated like a fixed rule.
misconceptions.fix: A budget should be reviewed and adjusted when income or expenses change, such as when prices go up.

probe.question: Prices of vegetables rise and the family income stays the same. Should the budget change?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a budget is fixed once made.

misconceptions.root_belief: a plan once made is fixed

misconceptions.statement: Saving is useless unless I can save a big amount.
misconceptions.why: Small amounts look too tiny to matter.
misconceptions.fix: Small amounts saved regularly build the saving habit and grow into a large sum over time.

probe.question: Is saving Rs 10 a day worth it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, Rs 10 is too small to matter.

misconceptions.root_belief: small amounts have no effect

misconceptions.statement: Savings are only for buying something I want, never for emergencies.
misconceptions.why: Children see saving as a way to get toys or gadgets.
misconceptions.fix: Savings are also kept for emergencies such as illness or sudden repairs, as well as for future goals.

probe.question: Why should a family keep some savings even if they have no buying plan?
probe.wrong_answer: There is no reason; savings are only for buying wants.

misconceptions.root_belief: one thing has only one purpose

misconceptions.statement: A piggy bank is as good as a bank account because it also keeps money safe and grows it.
misconceptions.why: Both are called banks and both store money.
misconceptions.fix: A piggy bank gives no interest, can be lost, stolen or spent easily, while a bank account is safe and earns interest.

probe.question: Which gives interest: a piggy bank or a bank savings account?
probe.wrong_answer: Both give interest.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Money put in a bank is gone, and the bank keeps it.
misconceptions.why: Children do not see the money after depositing it.
misconceptions.fix: Deposited money still belongs to the account holder, who can withdraw it when needed.

probe.question: Ria deposits Rs 500 in her bank account. Can she take it back later?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the bank keeps it.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about banks and economic institutions

misconceptions.statement: The bank keeps my actual notes in a box with my name on it.
misconceptions.why: Children imagine a bank as a bigger piggy bank.
misconceptions.fix: The bank records your balance in its books, and uses deposits to give loans. It returns the same amount, not the same notes, when you withdraw.

probe.question: When Sam withdraws Rs 100, does he get the very same note he deposited?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the bank keeps his own notes.

misconceptions.root_belief: a bank is a bigger piggy bank
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about how banks work

misconceptions.statement: Banks give interest for free as a gift, and it does not depend on the amount or time.
misconceptions.why: Interest is received without visible effort.
misconceptions.fix: Interest is a payment by the bank for using your money, and it depends on the amount, the rate and the time.

probe.question: Will Rs 1000 kept for 1 year earn the same interest as Rs 5000 kept for 1 year at the same rate?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the interest is the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Saving Rs 10 a day gives only Rs 10 in the end, not a bigger amount.
misconceptions.why: Students look at each deposit and not the total.
misconceptions.fix: Rs 10 saved every day adds up: in 365 days it is Rs 3650.

probe.question: How much will Rs 10 saved every day be after 30 days?
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 10.

misconceptions.root_belief: small amounts have no effect

misconceptions.statement: Compound interest means the interest is the same every year.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse it with simple interest.
misconceptions.fix: In compound interest, interest is added to the money and then earns interest too, so each year's interest is larger. In simple interest, it stays the same each year.

probe.question: Rs 1000 at 10 percent compound interest: is the interest in year 2 the same as year 1?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, Rs 100 both years.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from simple cases works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student difficulties with exponential growth and compound interest

misconceptions.statement: Money in a bank account grows only if I keep adding money.
misconceptions.why: Students see growth as coming only from deposits.
misconceptions.fix: Even without new deposits, money in a bank earns interest and grows.

probe.question: Rs 1000 stays in a savings account for a year with no new deposits. Will it grow?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it stays Rs 1000.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
